::: {.why}
Trading games are the round where academics do worst, and the reason is that they are treated as puzzles rather than as decisions with an explicit objective.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State what a quote width is trading off and what a skew is expressing, in one sentence each.
- Quote and requote on three exercises, saying the reasoning out loud each time.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Write the two objectives precisely: width trades the probability of trading against the expected loss to someone better informed, and skew expresses your inventory and your view about the fair value. Then note the third thing a width does, which is to protect against your own estimate being wrong, and which is the one candidates forget.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Practise three exercises out loud, quoting a two-sided market on a quantity, being traded with, and requoting. Say the reasoning at each step. Recording yourself once is worth more than doing six silently, because the assessment in a real interview is of the reasoning rather than of the number.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
The two objectives written precisely, plus a recording of three quote-and-requote exercises with reasoning spoken.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
I lift your offer twice in a row. What do you do to your quote, and what are you assuming when you do it?
:::
